abstract: Drug-safety information systems must distinguish direct bile salt export pump (BSEP) inhibition from transcriptional changes in hepatic transport programs. We investigated whether repression of ABCB11, which encodes BSEP, tracks an integrated stress response (ISR) after accounting for dose and liver-identity proxies. We analyzed 197 human hepatocyte RNA-seq dose conditions for 50 compounds using compound-centered models and 2,000 compound-bootstrap resamples. The association remained negative after dose and 436-gene identity adjustment ($β=-0.288$; 95\% interval, $-0.416$ to $-0.127$), and after jointly adding global-expression, oxidative-stress and apoptosis scores ($β=-0.198$; $-0.342$ to $-0.039$). The adjusted partial correlation ($r=-0.422$) exceeded in absolute magnitude those obtained for all but 1 of 5,000 expression-matched and 16 of 5,000 expression- and variance-matched random six-gene sets. Several comparator transporters also declined, indicating that the association was not restricted to ABCB11. Adding an interpolated source-screen viability proxy to all controls retained a negative estimate but an interval including zero ($β=-0.190$; $-0.335$ to $0.009$; 152 conditions, 39 compounds). Exposure-restricted uncertainty likewise depended on identity adjustment. Published modules from 240 external microarray conditions for 80 perturbagens showed consistent stress--metabolic covariation, without gene-level replication. A separate assay/FDA audit exposed sparse joint coverage and source-dependent associations. Together, these analyses link hepatocyte stress to ABCB11 repression and provide a biologically grounded approach to integrating biochemical, transcriptional and regulatory evidence for drug-safety assessment.
